blocks.text: His supervisor was standing ten feet away, next to an FBI agent. She looked at him and said quietly, "No, you don't, Gary."
The agents seized his computer and two external hard drives from his desk drawer. Gary sat down in the nearest chair and didn't say another word.

The investigation took five months. Gary had worked at the pension fund for twenty-two years. His job included handling survivor benefit claims for widows and widowers. He picked people who were elderly, grieving, and alone, people who often didn't speak English as their first language or didn't understand the forms. Then he filed forged waivers in their names, declaring that they'd given up their spouse's pension.
The unclaimed money sat in a holding account, and Gary quietly transferred it, a little at a time, to an account he'd opened under his late mother's name.
Mrs. Alvarez was one of twenty-three victims. In total, he'd taken more than one point four million dollars.
He pleaded guilty to federal wire fraud and forgery. The pension fund hired an outside firm to review every waiver signed in the last fifteen years.

Mrs. Alvarez received six years of survivor benefits in a single check, with interest. She paid off her property taxes the same week. Then she went to the church food pantry that had fed her through those years and wrote them a check for a thousand dollars.
She still goes to the pantry every Thursday. But now she's behind the table, handing out groceries.
She keeps her old wrist X-ray in a frame on her bookshelf, beside a photo of her husband. "That broken wrist," she likes to say, "was the luckiest accident of my life."
If you think an older relative is a victim of financial exploitation, the Eldercare Locator can help at 1-800-677-1116.
